paras: The lynching of Wise was the hanging of an accused horse thief by settlers in the Turtle Mountains of Dakota on Wednesday, September 12, 1888. According to accounts relayed from Bismarck, several settlers who had missed horses overtook him on his way to Manitoba, disarmed him, and hanged him from the nearest tree. Papers across the country carried the story because the dead man was said to have once been a prominent citizen of Wyoming mentioned for its legislature.

Settlers in the Turtle Mountains had been missing stock for some time and were watching for the thief, according to the Bismarck Tribune. The wire account added that many animals missed in the vicinity were believed to have been taken across the border by Wise. He was said to have come from Pennsylvania, where his family still lived, and to have been well known along the Northern Pacific before settling in Dakota.

On Wednesday several settlers caught up with Wise in a ravine as he drove a herd of horses toward the Canadian line. He first "showed fight" and tried to raise his rifle, the Tribune said, but the pursuers had their weapons ready and he dropped it, put up his hands, and gave up the stock. He was then taken to the nearest tree and hanged.
The only source for these details was a private letter from the scene, and the Tribune remarked that the affair had "been kept pretty quiet in the upper country."
No report of an inquest, arrest, or any official action appears in the coverage, and none of the settlers was named.

The story reached the press as a Bismarck special dated September 14, printed the next day by the New-York Tribune and the St. Paul Daily Globe, and as a Chicago relay carried by the Washington Evening Star and the Alexandria Gazette. Headlines dwelt on the fall of a once-respectable man: the New-York Tribune ran "A Politician Lynched for Horse Stealing," the Evening Star "A Once Prominent Citizen of Wyoming Hanged for Horse Stealing," and the Camden Evening Telegram "A Superior Horse Thief." The Globe headed its version "Hanged to a Tree" and called the killing "Summary Punishment Meted Out to a Horse Thief," and no paper questioned the accusation or the absence of a trial.

Over the next days the full text ran in papers such as the Wichita Eagle, while the Savannah Morning News and the Wheeling Sunday Register printed shorter versions. Weekly papers reduced it to one line in their news summaries, where it was dated "on the 14th" in Minnesota and Dakota weeklies and "on Friday" in the Chicago Citizen. Inside Dakota, the Hand County Press ran it as "Lynched a Horse-Thief" and the Jamestown Weekly Alert reprinted the Bismarck Tribune's account, the only one to give the name John Wise. The item still circulated weeks later, as a one-line note in the Southern Herald of Liberty, Mississippi, and as a brief in the Abbeville Press and Banner on October 10.

The date varied in reprinting: the Bismarck dispatches and the Tribune said Wednesday, a New Hampshire summary said Thursday, and the Camden paper said only "one day the past week." Condensed briefs placed the hanging in the "Turtle Creek Mountains" rather than the Turtle Mountains.

bases: Settlers who had missed horses overtook Wise, disarmed him, took back the horses, and hanged him from the nearest tree for alleged horse stealing (A2, A12, A15).
Every report says Wise was 'lynched' by 'several settlers' who hanged him at the nearest tree without any legal process, for alleged horse stealing (A2, A12, A15); 'several' gives no exact number.

The wire dispatches and the Bismarck Tribune all trace the story to 'private advices' or 'a private letter' from the Turtle Mountains (A2, A15); no local or independent account, inquest or denial appears.

accounts.gist: Several settlers who had missed horses overtook Wise in a ravine en route to Manitoba; he showed fight, was forced to throw down his rifle and surrender the horses, and was driven to the nearest tree and lynched.

accounts.label: Bismarck Tribune (private letter)
accounts.gist: Settlers missing stock overtook 'John Wise' on Wednesday driving stolen horses toward the Canadian line; he tried to raise his rifle but was covered, surrendered, and was escorted to the nearest tree and lynched; the affair had been 'kept pretty quiet in the upper country'.

framing.detail: Telegraph headlines played on the contrast between the victim's past and his end: 'A POLITICIAN LYNCHED FOR HORSE STEALING', 'A ONCE PROMINENT CITIZEN OF WYOMING HANGED FOR HORSE STEALING', 'A SUPERIOR HORSE THIEF'.
The St. Paul Globe called the hanging 'Summary Punishment Meted Out to a Horse Thief' and every paper treated the theft as established, with no comment on the lack of a trial.
Weekly papers ran the item as a single line in news summaries, often with the date changed.

conflicts.note: The Bismarck dispatches dated Sept. 14 and the Bismarck Tribune agree on Wednesday; the 'on the 14th' summaries, which date every item by its dispatch, and the 'Friday' rewrite appear to use the dispatch date, so Wednesday is the better-supported date.
'Turtle Creek' appears only in condensed briefs and looks like an editing slip.
Only the Bismarck Tribune gives a first name. A Pennsylvania report about ex-congressman Morgan R. Wise being lynched 'in Arizona or Montana' (A31) is not connected to Dakota by any paper.
